senses: Often Merlion: a symbolic creature having the head of a lion and the body of a fish, which is a national symbol of Singapore; an image, statue, or other depiction of this creature.
A fictional creature of similar make-up.
ety: From mer- + lion; sense 1 promoted by the Singapore Tourism Board as the name of a statue installed at the mouth of the Singapore River on 15 September 1972.
examples: And in the fourteenth century / Because of Nila Utama's river mouth encounter with a merlion / The Lion City surged into being / And its people could travel the wide world
There were night penguins that emitted green light only when hunting in dark seas, and merlions whose manes were fringed with pallid lavender.

senses: The state or characteristic of being persistent.
A measure of how much something persists.
ety: From persist + -ency.
examples: On entering her room he had been struck by the absence of that saucy independence usually apparent in her bearing towards him, notwithstanding the persistency with which he had hovered near her for the previous month.
However that may be, the hostility of the comic writers had evidently a general hostility behind it. Our tradition states this definitely and the persistency of the attacks proves it.

senses: Feeling pain or sorrow on account of one's sins or offenses; feeling sincere guilt.
Doing penance.
ety: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin paenitēns, poenitēns (“penitent”), present participle of paeniteō, poeniteō (“to cause to repent; to regret, repent”). Doublet of penitente.
examples: Be penitent, and for thy fault contrite.

senses: An edible jelly made from this material.
A thin, translucent membrane used as a filter for photography or for theatrical lighting effects.
ety: Borrowed from French gélatine (“jelly, gel”), from Italian gelatina (“jelly, gel”), from gelare (“to freeze”), from Latin gelō (“to freeze”).
examples: For both images I placed a Kodak 4.0 neutral-density gelatin filter over the lens to reduce the Sun's brightness.

senses: To attract and delight, to charm.
To cast a spell upon (often one that attracts or charms).
To magically enhance or degrade an item.
ety: From Middle English enchaunten, from Old French enchanter, from Latin incantāre. Doublet of incant.
examples: With the aid of his eponymous pipes, a satyr is capable of weaving a wide variety of melodic spells designed to enchant others and bring them in line with his capricious desires.

senses: A female giant.
ety: From Middle English geauntesse, geaunesse, from Old French; equivalent to giant + -ess.
examples: In the corner lay against the wall a stringed instrument not unlike a dulcimer, which, as people believe, the Giantesses used to play on.
The giantess picked him up and gave him such a squeeze that he felt he was going to choke.
The giantesses lift arms like the trunks of sycamores, each finger tipped with an amaranthine talon.

senses: A place for gathering.
A marketplace, especially in Classical Greece.
ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀγορά (agorá).
examples: The custom was to dance its length, moving from partner to masked partner all the way to the agora, the city’s gathering place.

senses: Able to be won or achieved.
ety: From win + -able.
examples: No winnable seat has been found for Mr. H. L. Nathan, a powerful recruit from the Liberal ranks, and poor Mr. Wedgwood Benn, an invaluable sniper for a party in Opposition, has been out of Parliament now since 1931.

senses: A region of shrubs, typically dry in the summer and rainy in the winter. The coast of the Mediterranean is such a region.
The foliage of creosote bush, Larrea divaricata, when used as a medicinal herb.
ety: From Spanish chaparral, from chaparro (“evergreen oak”) + -al, from Basque txaparro, from txapar, from sapar.
examples: It was quite dark when, after an arduous climb, the sheriff made his tortuous way through the chaparral to the point where Anthony Garland should be stationed.
Have you ever been south of Monterey? / Barrancas carve the coastline / And the chaparral flows to the sea / 'Neath waves of golden sunshine

senses: The thick end, especially of a piece of wood or of a joint of meat.
ety: Origin uncertain; probably a blend of chunk and lump or stump, or perhaps a nasalised variant of chub (“someone chubby, something thick”). Compare Icelandic kubbur (“block of wood, chip (computing)”), Old Norse kumbr for kubbr (“block of wood”), English chop.
examples: Shaped as if they had been unskilfully cut off the chump-end of something.

senses: That which makes sure; that which confirms; ground of confidence or security.
A substitute; a hostage.
Evidence; confirmation; warrant.
ety: From Middle English surete, attested since the early 1300s in the sense "guarantee, promise, pledge, assurance", from Anglo-Norman seurté/Old French seurté with the same meaning (whence modern French sûreté), from Latin sēcūritās. Equivalent to sure + -ty. The senses "security, safety, stability" and "certainty" are attested since the late 1300s. "One who undertakes to pay if another does not" is from the early 1400s. Doublet of security.
examples: She called the saints to surety, That she would never put it from her finger, Unless she gave it to yourself.

senses: In a state of astonishment, wonder, expectation, or eager attention; as with mouth hanging open.
ety: From a- + gape. First known use by John Milton in Paradise Lost (1667).
examples: There I stand, agape like any country bumpkin
That's all well and good; one can sit, agape, reading the copious liner notes to this or any Explorer record, but it's what's inside the jacket that counts.
The restaurant staff and OTHER DINNER GUESTS watch, agape.

senses: To put (something such as a knife or sword) into a sheath.
To encase (something) with a protective covering.
Of an animal: to draw back or retract (a body part) into the body, such as claws into a paw.
To thrust (a sharp object like a sword, a claw, or a tusk) into something.
ety: From Late Middle English shethen (“to put (a sword or knife) into a sheath, sheathe; to provide with a sheath; (figuratively) to have sexual intercourse”) [and other forms], then: * probably from Old English *scēaþian; or * possibly from Middle English sheth, shethe (“holder for a sword, knife, etc., scabbard, sheath”) [and other forms] + -en (suffix forming the infinitive of verbs). Sheth(e) is derived from Old English sċēaþ (“sheath”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaiþiju, from Proto-Germanic *skaiþiz (“sheath; covering”), from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to dissect, split”) (possibly from th
examples: Be aware of the smiling enemy, that openly sheatheth his weapon, / But mingleth poison in secret with the sacred salt of hospitality.
She sheathed her legs in the sheerest of the nylons that her father had brought back from the Continent, and slipped her feet into the toeless, high-heeled shoes of black suède.
But he could never come up with enough enchantment or dream material to sheathe himself in. It would not cover.

senses: Full of chinks, laden with small cracks or openings.
Resembling a chink sound.
ety: From chink (“crack”) + -y.
examples: The door was knockerless and chinky, and creaked dismally as I inserted the key.
The money made a chinky sound as I shook the purse.

senses: The escape of gas from solution in a liquid, especially the escape of carbon dioxide from a carbonated drink.
Fomentation.
ety: Borrowed from French effervescence. By surface analysis, ef- + Latin ferv- + -escence.
examples: We are in the habit of calling those bodies of men anarchal which are in a state of effervescence.

senses: Someone who is materialistic, concerned only with material possessions.
A follower or proponent of philosophical materialism.
ety: From material + -ist.
examples: Ironically, today's generation has become the little materialists and "fame whores" (New York Magazine's term) their boomer parents so reviled.

senses: An ambush; a trap laid for an enemy.
The place in which troops lie hidden for an ambush.
The body of troops lying in ambush.
ety: From French embuscade, from Italian imboscata from the past participle of imboscare (“to ambush”), from Vulgar Latin *imbosco (“I hide, ambush”) (see there for more), from Frankish *busk (“bush”), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“bush, heavy stick”). Compare ambush. More at bush.
examples: The yellow cat deliberately stretched himself, yawned, and followed; and proceeded to carry out a wonderful scheme of feints and ambuscades in regard to a ping-pong ball which was kept for his proper diversion.
I went so far with it in my Imagination, that I employed my self several days to find out proper Places to put my self in Ambuscade

senses: An exhibition in which one (typically much stronger) player plays several games at the same time against different opponents.
ety: Abbreviation of simultaneous.
examples: We're not just starting with Round 1. We're kicking off with a simul. Four simuls to be exact.
He could have organized a simul with a rat without blinking an eye.
I saw Glenn wrapping up his speech, and told Baynes to come back that evening for the simul.

senses: A bowl-shaped geographical feature formed by glaciation.
ety: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic coire.
examples: Fleet foot on the correi, / Sage counsel in cumber, Red hand in the foray, / How sound is thy slumber!

senses: A unit of measurement that measures a material's absorbance of sound. A material that is 1 square meter in size that can absorb 100% of sound has a value of one metric sabin.
ety: From Wallace Clement Sabine (1868-1919), US physicist.
examples: Sabine gave his name to the sabin, the standard unit that is ‘equal to the sound absorption of a square foot of a perfectly absorbing surface such as an open window’.

senses: A Bavarian specialty beer in which a significant proportion of malted barley is replaced with malted wheat.
ety: Borrowed from German Weißbier, probably from weiß (“white”) + Bier (“beer”), but see the lemma.
examples: It actually starts as two beers, Mr. Adrià said: a straightforward lager and a German-style weissbier that is seasoned with orange peel, coriander and licorice.

senses: To exhibit alliteration.
To use (a word or sound) so as to make alliteration.
ety: Back-formation from alliteration.
examples: It is a strophe of six lines, of which the first and second and the fourth and fifth belong together, while the third and sixth are independently alliterated.

senses: Someone who spreads fear.
ety: From fear + monger (“dealer in a specific commodity; (by extension) person promoting something undesirable”).
examples: I think the Tea Partiers, despite their contradictions, are not all wrong about Big Government. But I worry that, in time, a clever fearmonger could manipulate popular opinion into an electoral mandate.

senses: Very baffling, confusing, or perplexing, often due to a very large choice being available.
ety: From bewilder (“to confuse, disorientate, or puzzle someone, especially with many different choices”) + -ing (suffix forming nouns or noun-like words from verbs, denoting the act of doing something, an action, or the embodiment of an action; and forming the present participles of verbs).
examples: There was a bewildering collection of curiosities filling the room.

senses: A magnifying glass, usually mounted in an eyepiece, often used by jewellers and watchmakers.
A type of short-range binoculars used by surgeons and dentists.
ety: Borrowed from French loupe.
examples: The watchmaker himself, a white-haired éminence grise, was bent over his work, a jeweler’s loupe in his eye, when I walked in.

senses: Pertaining, similar, or belonging to a germ.
Serving as a point of origin; formative.
Highly influential; seminal.
ety: From oblique stem of Latin germen, germinis (“seed”) + -al.
examples: My upbringing was the germinal idea behind the opera.
This case was germinal to development of the theory of joint participation.

senses: An Ancient Greek drinking cup with a stem, two handles, and a broad, shallow body.
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek κύλιξ (kúlix, “cup”).
examples: The dig team unearthed a kylix at the site in Bergama.

senses: A rich sauce, made of chocolate and cream, used also as the filling of truffles, and as a glaze.
A kind of surcoat with short cap sleeves.
ety: Borrowed from French ganache, from Italian ganascia (“jaw”), ultimately from Ancient Greek γνάθος (gnáthos) (see gnatho-).
examples: The centers of truffles are typically a ganache, which is most often simply a mixture of chocolate and cream. The recipes will direct you to chop the chocolate finely—do not overlook this step!
She scoops a grassy, barely sweet green-tea sorbet onto white chocolate ganache, and garnishes it with coin-size meringues that break easily, then strings syrupy, candied yuzu zest across it all.

senses: The condition or character of a queen; queenly rule, power, or authority.
A realm ruled by a queen.
The subjects of such a realm.
ety: From queen + -dom.
examples: She was the fairest maiden in all the queendom.
The whole queendom was outraged by the diplomatic slight.

senses: Having the characteristics of propaganda; spreading propaganda.
ety: From propagandist + -ic or propaganda + -istic.
examples: For this reason some overfamiliar or recycled accounts provoke boredom or disbelief, and can be made to seem propagandistic.

senses: Introductory or preparatory.
Influencing; tending to induce or cause.
ety: From Middle French inductif, from Late Latin inductivus.
examples: A brutish vice, / Inductive mainly to the sin of Eve.

senses: A person or a thing which brings something.
Someone who supplies or identifies potential recruits for the military in exchange for payment.
ety: From bring + -er.
examples: Yet the first bringer of unwelcome news / Hath but a losing office.

senses: Loose stony debris on a slope.
Similar debris made up of broken building material such as bricks, concrete, etc.
A slope made up of scree at the base of a cliff, mountain, etc.
ety: Probably a back-formation from screes, from Old Norse skriða (“landslide, landslip”); compare skríða (“to glide”) (from Proto-Germanic *skrīþaną (“to crawl; to glide; to walk”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kreyt-, *(s)ker- (“to bend, turn”)). The word is cognate with Icelandic skriða (“avalanche; landslide, landslip; steep mountain- or hillside made up of gravel and loose rocks”).
examples: To the north the towering scree-strewn slopes of Saddleback begin to draw nearer as we start the abrupt descent towards Keswick.
Struggling down the slope, There's not much hope. I begin to try to ride the scree But the rocks are tumbling all around me.

Acres of the industrial port had been reduced to desolation, half-walls, half-chimneys, crazy sticks of steel that looped up out of concrete scree. The temptation not to clear and rebuild must have been strong.

senses: A net used to catch fish.
A fabric mesh with an open diamond-shaped structure.
Stockings made of fishnet fabric.
ety: From Middle English fishnet; equivalent to fish + net.
examples: The fishnets were hung over bushes to dry.

All the little minnows which were not caught for bait this spring may well give thanks to the women of the U. S. who have adopted fishnet turbans, scarfs, belts and skirts as items in their sports outfits.
Fishnets are for catching men.

senses: A thick tortilla as made in Mexico, frequently stuffed and made of corn flour.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish gordita.
examples: The term gordita means “little fat tortilla” and all gorditas are made from masa, but what you are served when you order a gordita will vary depending on where you are in Mexico.

senses: spacious; having much space
of, related to or connected with the extraterrestrial
ety: From space + -y.
examples: His latest CD sounds very spacy.

senses: A musical genre that is a fusion of psytrance and ambient.
ety: Blend of psytrance + ambient.
examples: Psybient artists include Shpongle, Entheogenic (2), Evan Bluetech, Yaniv Shulman, Kickbong, and some of the works of Younger Brother.

senses: Inclined to make (disapproving) judgments; judgmental.
ety: From judge + -y, late 2000s.
examples: But when he just announced, matter-of-factly, that he really liked pot, and hash, and acid, and speed, and meth, and coke, well…it kind of seemed like, I don't know, everybody has a hobby. I shouldn't be so judgy.
Riley lowered his eyebrows and crossed his arms and tried to look non-judgy even if he felt a little judgy.

senses: Living in or among trees.
Covered or filled with trees.
ety: From Latin arboreus (“tree-like”) + -al, mid-17th century.
examples: If the harvest mouse had been more strictly arboreal, it would perhaps have had its tail rendered structurally prehensile, as is the case with some members of the same order.
An arboreal animal which makes itself at home in genealogical trees.
The breadth of the arboreal landscape requires a longer list of living creatures, and creatures of greater bulk.

senses: To make furious or mad with anger; to fill with fury.
ety: First attested in 1667; borrowed from Medieval Latin infuriātus (“enraged”), perfect passive participle of infuriō (“to enrage”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin furia (“rage, fury, frenzy”); perhaps via Italian infuriato.
examples: What graceles fears, strange hates, may Nations so affright, Infuriate so; gainst God with mad attempts to fight?
US House Speaker Nancy Pelosi has left Taiwan after a one-day visit that has infuriated China.
